newsitem.title: MEXICO: Tensions cast shadow over Clinton visit to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Tensions cast shadow over Clinton visit to Mexico.

text.p: Tensions over drugs and immigration clouded the atmosphere on Monday ahead of President Bill Clinton's first visit to Mexico.
Clinton, the first U.S. president to visit Mexico City since Jimmy Carter in 1979, was to arrive in the Mexican capital at 6:35 p.m. local time (2335 GMT), at the start of his tour of Latin America.

Members of Clinton's Cabinet, including Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, arrived ahead of the president for a meeting Monday afternoon of the U.S.-Mexico Binational Commission -- a permanent body that coordinates work between the two governments on a wide range of issues.

"These meetings are an occasion to put on record the agreements and also to resolve the disagreements, to take stock of the work we have done and also to plan things going forward" Mexican foreign minister Jose Angel Gurria told local television.
Helped by the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), trade between the United States and Mexico reached a record $140 billion last year.
But Mexico is also the main source of two U.S. problems -- illegal immigrants and illegal drugs.

Tensions between the two countries have risen sharply in recent months. New U.S. measures to crack down on illegal migrants have upset Mexico and high-level drug corruption in Mexico has angered Washington.

Mexican government officials tried to sound upbeat about the visit but admitted that tough discussions on the two prickliest topics of the agenda -- drugs and migration -- were likely to steal the headlines.

"The coverage is inevitably going to reflect the fact that topics are being discussed which are conflictive," one Mexican official said. "But we hope we will also see the positive aspects of the relationship and the things we have achieved."

Reflecting the importance of the drug issue, U.S. ambassador to Mexico James Jones warned in unusually frank comments to Newsweek magazine that Mexico risked turning into another Colombia if it did not crack down fast on narcotics.
"My sense is you have a three- to five-year period to bring law and order back into the system or Mexico could become another Colombia," Jones told Newsweek.
"If cartels permeate society, then you don't have a democratic system and everything you want to accomplish to have First World status goes down the drain."

U.S. officials have asked for permission to arm Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agents operating in Mexico but Mexican president Ernesto Zedillo flatly ruled that out in an interview last Friday.

Army troops and police clamped tight security on the area around the Presidente Intercontinental hotel where Clinton was to stay and gathered outside the U.S. Embassy on the city's main avenue Reforma.
Riot police massed discreetly on side roads around the hotel area and security officials told Reuters plain clothes officers were also active.

Ahead of the president's arrival, members of the debtors' group El Barzon briefly draped a black ribbon around the Angel of Independence monument on Reforma Monday morning before police asked them to take it down.

"We are dressing our homeland in mourning," Barzon leader Jose Maria Imaz said. "Today ... after the Battle of Puebla in which foreigners were expelled from Mexico, Clinton is coming here ... they have chosen a wicked date for Clinton's visit."
Mexico was celebrating Monday the 135th anniversary of the Battle of Puebla, when government troops defeated the invading French.
More highbrow commentators also noted the irony of a visit by Mexico's all-powerful northern neighbour beginning on a day when the country remembered a battle against foreigners.

"President Clinton arrives today in Mexico on a date which reminds us strongly of our painful relationship with countries possessing the power to subjugate (others)," left-wing commentator Miguel Angel Granados Chapa wrote in the daily newspaper Reforma.
